notes: Each eval points the skill at the fixture agent system under graph-system-document-workspace/fixtures/ and asks for its guide. The fixture carries deliberate traps: ops/notes.md contradicts the code on resumability and on the repair bound, the traces exercise only the happy path, POST /runs has no auth, and nothing wires up the alerting the notes claim. Expectations assert on evidence honesty, content coverage, HTML self-containment, visual discipline and proportionate process — not on wording or section order, since two competent runs will structure a guide differently and both be right. The load-bearing expectations are the negative ones: no invented security controls, no declared behavior narrated as observed, no diagram asserting an edge the code does not contain, no silent omission. Evals 3 and 4 exist because the cheapest ways to fail this specification are to over-produce a small job and to regenerate a document that only needed a patch.

evals.name: full-guide-from-repo-only-evidence
evals.prompt: We're onboarding a new maintainer onto our nightly ingestion agent next week and there's no documentation at all. Can you write a proper architecture and operations guide for it? Everything's in this directory — the graph is in src/graph.py, prompts under prompts/, deploy stuff in deploy/, some hand-kept notes in ops/notes.md and a couple of run logs in logs/. Put it in docs/. There's no staging access from here so you can only go off what's in the repo.
evals.expected_output: A self-contained HTML guide in docs/ covering all thirteen content areas or marking them not applicable with a reason, with claims labeled declared/observed/inferred/unknown, at least one generated diagram carrying takeaway/scope/evidence/text-equivalent, a source register, and a verification summary naming unresolved gaps.
expectations: The deliverable is a single self-contained HTML file in docs/ that loads no remote stylesheet, font, script or image.
The page declares html lang, a viewport meta and a non-empty title, and remains complete and navigable with JavaScript disabled.
The guide covers every required content area, or explicitly marks an area not applicable with a stated reason — no area is silently dropped.
At least one diagram is rendered as inline SVG and appears inside a figure with a caption stating title, takeaway, scope and evidence status, plus a text-equivalent table.

The run-path diagram matches src/graph.py: five working nodes plus give_up, the conditional route out of validate, and the repair back-edge bounded at INGEST_MAX_REPAIR (2) — no edge or node the code does not contain.
Claims are labeled by evidence state, and behavior read from code, config or prompts is labeled declared rather than presented as observed.
Behavior demonstrated by logs/run-2026-07-14.jsonl is labeled observed with its scope named, and the guide states that the repair, give_up and failure paths were never exercised by those traces.

The conflict between ops/notes.md ("always picks up where it left off", "retries three times") and the code (Postgres checkpointer, INGEST_MAX_REPAIR default 2) is surfaced as a finding rather than silently resolved.
The security section reports the absence of authentication on POST /runs as a verified gap, citing src/serve.py and deploy/docker-compose.yml.

No security control is asserted generically (no unsupported 'encrypted at rest, RBAC, secrets in a vault' boilerplate), and no secret, credential or interpolated password value appears in the deliverable.
The observability section names the blind spot that no metrics, traces or alerting exist despite ops/notes.md claiming alerts go to #data-eng.
A source register produced by scripts/source_register.py records path, revision and freshness for the sources inspected.
scripts/verify_doc.py is run against the deliverable and its failures are addressed or reported, with repair stopping at two attempts for the same failure.
The file is written into docs/ without asking permission first, since it is a new file inside the authorized location.

evals.name: operator-facing-runbook-depth
evals.prompt: Our on-call rotation keeps getting paged for this nightly ingestion agent and nobody except me knows how to recover it. I need a system guide they can actually use at 3am — what it does, how to tell it's broken, what they're allowed to restart and what they must not touch. Code's in src/, the runbook fragments we have are in ops/notes.md, and there are traces in logs/ from last month's runs. Make it something someone will actually read under pressure.
evals.expected_output: An operator-oriented HTML guide: what healthy looks like, stop conditions and prohibited actions reachable without scrolling through the whole document, triage, safe start/stop/resume, escalation, observability blind spots — with traced behavior labeled observed and its scope named, and declared behavior kept distinct.
expectations: Stop-and-escalate conditions and prohibited actions are visually prominent and reachable early, not buried in the last section a reader would scroll to.
The operations section states prerequisites, permitted roles, safe start/stop/trigger procedures, and the observable signature of a healthy run.
Recovery covers resume-from-checkpoint semantics accurately: the Postgres checkpointer means a run can resume by thread_id, contradicting nothing the code shows.
The guide names the conditions under which an operator must stop and escalate rather than continuing.
Behavior demonstrated by the traces is labeled observed with its time window or run ids named, including which paths the traces did not exercise.
Behavior read only from code or ops/notes.md is labeled declared and is not presented as demonstrated.
The observability section names blind spots — no metrics, no traces, no wired alerting — rather than describing aspirational monitoring.
Conflicts between ops/notes.md and the code are surfaced as findings rather than silently resolved in favour of one.
The guide still covers the other required content areas rather than narrowing to a runbook, or states a reason for any area marked not applicable.

Diagrams appear only where they answer a reader question prose would answer worse; each carries title, takeaway, scope, evidence status and a text equivalent, and none encodes meaning by colour alone.
The page prints legibly: a print stylesheet exists and collapsed disclosures do not hide operational content in print.

evals.name: small-job-stays-cheap
evals.prompt: Quick one — can you document the little retry wrapper in tools/retry_agent.py? It's about 40 lines, one function, no deployment story, we run it by hand. Just needs to be enough that someone else can pick it up.
evals.expected_output: A short but complete guide proportionate to a 40-line hand-run tool: applicable areas covered with real detail, inapplicable ones marked with reasons, no invented content and no assurance machinery beyond the default workflow.
expectations: Areas that genuinely do not apply (deployment topology, HA, observability infrastructure, graph behavior) are marked not applicable with a stated reason rather than padded with invented content.
Areas that do apply — purpose, contract, inputs and outputs, configuration, retry and failure semantics, limitations — are covered with real detail from the file.
The retry semantics are documented specifically and correctly: three attempts on validation failure with 2/8/30 second backoff, and transport errors deliberately not caught.

The format choice is proportionate and briefly justified rather than agonised over; if HTML is produced it is still self-contained and passes the gates, and if Markdown is chosen the reason is stated in one line.
No diagram is produced merely to have one, or if one is produced it answers a question the prose does not.

No persisted claim registry, canonical JSON handoff artifact, approval gate for drafting, or multi-stage artifact chain is introduced — none of the escalation triggers apply and the run does not invent one.
No approval is requested before writing the new file.
A verification summary is still produced, however brief.
The run is materially cheaper than the full-guide runs in tokens and wall time.

evals.name: update-patches-rather-than-regenerates
evals.prompt: The system doc at docs/system-guide.html is a few months old. Since then we moved the checkpointer from in-memory to Postgres, added a give_up terminal node so a run that can't pass validation stops instead of looping, dropped the repair bound to 2, and swapped the summarizer model. Update it — don't rewrite the whole thing, the rest was reviewed and is fine.
evals.expected_output: A targeted update: changed sources identified by comparing registers, only affected sections and the run-path diagram revised, unaffected reviewed material preserved, stale claims removed rather than inherited, and a semantic diff presented before overwriting.
expectations: The run compares current sources against the previously recorded register or the existing guide rather than re-deriving the whole document from scratch.
Only the sections the changed evidence touches are revised — graph behavior, route contracts, node contracts, state persistence, models, configuration, operations and recovery.
Reviewed sections whose evidence did not change are preserved rather than reworded.

Claims contradicted by the new evidence are removed, not carried forward: in-memory checkpointing, 'nothing survives a restart', the max-3 repair bound, and the old summarizer model no longer appear as current behavior anywhere, including in the at-a-glance cards and the stop-conditions box.
The run-path diagram is re-rendered to include the give_up terminal node and the corrected repair bound, and its text equivalent is updated to match.
Only the affected visual is re-rendered; unaffected content is not regenerated.
The repair back-edge is documented with its trigger and its bound, and the terminal failure semantics of give_up (no partial bundle written) are stated.
The recovery guidance is corrected: a run can now resume from the Postgres checkpoint, so the previous 'restarting abandons the run' instruction is not left standing.
A concise semantic diff and its risks are presented to the user and approval is obtained before the existing file is overwritten.
The freshness and verification section is updated to reflect the new inspection date and revision, and the deliverable still passes verify_doc.py.
